claim: Individual animals vary in their behaviors even when they share the same genotype and were reared in the same environment.
source: Individual animals vary in their behaviors. This is true even when they share the same genotype and were reared in the same environment.
evidence: This is a foundational statement in the abstract that frames the research question, drawing on established scientific knowledge about behavioral variation.

claim: Clusters of covarying behaviors constitute behavioral syndromes.
source: Clusters of covarying behaviors constitute behavioral syndromes, and an individual's position along such axes of covariation is a representation of their personality.
evidence: This statement reflects established terminology and conceptual frameworks in behavioral ecology.

claim: The structure of behavioral covariation within a genotype is essentially uncharacterized.
source: Despite these conceptual frameworks, the structure of behavioral covariation within a genotype is essentially uncharacterized and its mechanistic origins unknown.
evidence: This is a knowledge gap statement that motivates the study, based on the authors' assessment of the literature.

claim: Hundreds of inbred Drosophila individuals were passed through an experimental pipeline that captured hundreds of behavioral measures.
source: Passing hundreds of inbred Drosophila individuals through an experimental pipeline that captured hundreds of behavioral measures, we found sparse but significant correlations among small sets of behaviors.
evidence: This describes the experimental design and data collection performed in the study.

claim: Sparse but significant correlations were found among small sets of behaviors in inbred Drosophila.
source: Passing hundreds of inbred Drosophila individuals through an experimental pipeline that captured hundreds of behavioral measures, we found sparse but significant correlations among small sets of behaviors.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data analysis.

claim: The space of behavioral variation has many independent dimensions.
source: Thus, the space of behavioral variation has many independent dimensions.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the finding of sparse correlations among behaviors.

claim: Manipulating the physiology of the brain and specific neural populations altered specific correlations between behaviors.
source: Manipulating the physiology of the brain, and specific neural populations, altered specific correlations.
evidence: This describes experimental results from neural manipulation experiments.

claim: Variation in gene expression can predict an individual's position on some behavioral axes.
source: We also observed that variation in gene expression can predict an individual's position on some behavioral axes.
evidence: This is a finding from the transcriptomic analysis and modeling.

claim: The Big Five personality traits model is frequently used by psychologists to describe the range of human personality.
source: A five-dimensional model (Goldberg, 1993) known as The Big Five personality traits is frequently used by psychologists to describe the range of human personality, and a similar model has been used to describe personality in fish (Réale et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to the literature.

claim: A similar model to the Big Five has been used to describe personality in fish.
source: A five-dimensional model (Goldberg, 1993) known as The Big Five personality traits is frequently used by psychologists to describe the range of human personality, and a similar model has been used to describe personality in fish (Réale et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Réale et al., 2007.

claim: Human propensity for behaviors such as assertiveness, talkativeness, and impulsiveness is collectively described as extraversion.
source: For example, human propensity for behaviors such as assertiveness, talkativeness, and impulsiveness is collectively described as extraversion and is thought to be anticorrelated with behaviors such as passivity, shyness, and deliberateness, all behaviors associated with introversion (Matthews et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Matthews et al., 2003.

claim: Extraversion is thought to be anticorrelated with introversion-associated behaviors such as passivity, shyness, and deliberateness.
source: For example, human propensity for behaviors such as assertiveness, talkativeness, and impulsiveness is collectively described as extraversion and is thought to be anticorrelated with behaviors such as passivity, shyness, and deliberateness, all behaviors associated with introversion (Matthews et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Matthews et al., 2003.

claim: Correlated aggressive and exploratory behaviors have been observed in insects.
source: Correlated aggressive and exploratory behaviors have been observed in insects (Jeanson and Weidenmüller, 2014), arachnids (Johnson and Sih, 2007), fish (Huntingford, 1976), and birds (van Oers et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Jeanson and Weidenmüller, 2014.

claim: Correlated aggressive and exploratory behaviors have been observed in arachnids.
source: Correlated aggressive and exploratory behaviors have been observed in insects (Jeanson and Weidenmüller, 2014), arachnids (Johnson and Sih, 2007), fish (Huntingford, 1976), and birds (van Oers et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Johnson and Sih, 2007.

claim: Correlated aggressive and exploratory behaviors have been observed in fish.
source: Correlated aggressive and exploratory behaviors have been observed in insects (Jeanson and Weidenmüller, 2014), arachnids (Johnson and Sih, 2007), fish (Huntingford, 1976), and birds (van Oers et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Huntingford, 1976.

claim: Correlated aggressive and exploratory behaviors have been observed in birds.
source: Correlated aggressive and exploratory behaviors have been observed in insects (Jeanson and Weidenmüller, 2014), arachnids (Johnson and Sih, 2007), fish (Huntingford, 1976), and birds (van Oers et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to van Oers et al., 2004.

claim: The prevalence of behavioral correlation in many species suggests that covariation is likely a universal feature of behavior.
source: The prevalence of behavioral correlation in so many species suggests that covariation is likely a universal feature of behavior.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited observations across multiple species.

claim: There is increasing evidence that substantial individual behavioral variation is rooted in intragenotypic variation.
source: But there is increasing evidence that substantial individual behavioral variation is rooted in intragenotypic variation (Honegger and de Bivort, 2018; Akhund-Zade et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Honegger and de Bivort, 2018 and Akhund-Zade et al., 2019.

claim: Substantial variation in specific behavioral measures has been observed in inbred lines of geckoes raised in standardized conditions.
source: Substantial variation in specific behavioral measures, even in inbred lines raised in standardized conditions, has been observed in several clonal animals, including geckoes (Sakai, 2018), amazonian mollies (Bierbach et al., 2017), and aphids and nematodes (Schuett et al., 2011; Stern et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Sakai, 2018.

claim: Substantial variation in specific behavioral measures has been observed in inbred lines of amazonian mollies raised in standardized conditions.
source: Substantial variation in specific behavioral measures, even in inbred lines raised in standardized conditions, has been observed in several clonal animals, including geckoes (Sakai, 2018), amazonian mollies (Bierbach et al., 2017), and aphids and nematodes (Schuett et al., 2011; Stern et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Bierbach et al., 2017.

claim: Substantial variation in specific behavioral measures has been observed in inbred lines of aphids and nematodes raised in standardized conditions.
source: Substantial variation in specific behavioral measures, even in inbred lines raised in standardized conditions, has been observed in several clonal animals, including geckoes (Sakai, 2018), amazonian mollies (Bierbach et al., 2017), and aphids and nematodes (Schuett et al., 2011; Stern et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Schuett et al., 2011 and Stern et al., 2017.

claim: Intragenotypic variability in behavior has been characterized in mice.
source: Genetic model systems hold particular promise for the mechanistic dissection of this variation, and intragenotypic variability (IGV) in behavior has been characterized in mice (Freund et al., 2013), zebrafish (Bierbach et al., 2017), and Drosophila.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Freund et al., 2013.

claim: Intragenotypic variability in behavior has been characterized in zebrafish.
source: Genetic model systems hold particular promise for the mechanistic dissection of this variation, and intragenotypic variability (IGV) in behavior has been characterized in mice (Freund et al., 2013), zebrafish (Bierbach et al., 2017), and Drosophila.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Bierbach et al., 2017.

claim: IGV of phototaxis has been studied in flies.
source: In flies, IGV of many behaviors has been studied, including phototaxis (Kain et al., 2012), locomotor handedness and wing-folding (Buchanan et al., 2015), spontaneous microbehaviors (Kain et al., 2013; Todd et al., 2017), thermal preference (Kain et al., 2015), and object-fixated locomotion (Linneweber et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kain et al., 2012.

claim: IGV of locomotor handedness and wing-folding has been studied in flies.
source: In flies, IGV of many behaviors has been studied, including phototaxis (Kain et al., 2012), locomotor handedness and wing-folding (Buchanan et al., 2015), spontaneous microbehaviors (Kain et al., 2013; Todd et al., 2017), thermal preference (Kain et al., 2015), and object-fixated locomotion (Linneweber et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Buchanan et al., 2015.

claim: IGV of spontaneous microbehaviors has been studied in flies.
source: In flies, IGV of many behaviors has been studied, including phototaxis (Kain et al., 2012), locomotor handedness and wing-folding (Buchanan et al., 2015), spontaneous microbehaviors (Kain et al., 2013; Todd et al., 2017), thermal preference (Kain et al., 2015), and object-fixated locomotion (Linneweber et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kain et al., 2013 and Todd et al., 2017.

claim: IGV of thermal preference has been studied in flies.
source: In flies, IGV of many behaviors has been studied, including phototaxis (Kain et al., 2012), locomotor handedness and wing-folding (Buchanan et al., 2015), spontaneous microbehaviors (Kain et al., 2013; Todd et al., 2017), thermal preference (Kain et al., 2015), and object-fixated locomotion (Linneweber et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kain et al., 2015.

claim: IGV of object-fixated locomotion has been studied in flies.
source: In flies, IGV of many behaviors has been studied, including phototaxis (Kain et al., 2012), locomotor handedness and wing-folding (Buchanan et al., 2015), spontaneous microbehaviors (Kain et al., 2013; Todd et al., 2017), thermal preference (Kain et al., 2015), and object-fixated locomotion (Linneweber et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Linneweber et al., 2020.

claim: Genetic variation underlies the magnitude of behavioral variability.
source: Mechanistic studies of these behavioral phenomena have addressed two major questions: (1) what biological mechanisms underlie the magnitude of behavioral variability (e.g., genetic variation [Ayroles et al., 2015] or neural state variation [Kain et al., 2012; Buchanan et al., 2015]), and (2) what specific differences within individual nervous systems predict individual behavioral biases (Linneweber et al., 2020; Mellert et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ayroles et al., 2015.

claim: Neural state variation underlies the magnitude of behavioral variability.
source: Mechanistic studies of these behavioral phenomena have addressed two major questions: (1) what biological mechanisms underlie the magnitude of behavioral variability (e.g., genetic variation [Ayroles et al., 2015] or neural state variation [Kain et al., 2012; Buchanan et al., 2015]), and (2) what specific differences within individual nervous systems predict individual behavioral biases (Linneweber et al., 2020; Mellert et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kain et al., 2012 and Buchanan et al., 2015.

claim: Specific differences within individual nervous systems predict individual behavioral biases.
source: Mechanistic studies of these behavioral phenomena have addressed two major questions: (1) what biological mechanisms underlie the magnitude of behavioral variability (e.g., genetic variation [Ayroles et al., 2015] or neural state variation [Kain et al., 2012; Buchanan et al., 2015]), and (2) what specific differences within individual nervous systems predict individual behavioral biases (Linneweber et al., 2020; Mellert et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Linneweber et al., 2020 and Mellert et al., 2016.

claim: No study to date has focused on characterizing the large-scale variance-covariance structure of IGV in behavior.
source: The mechanistic basis of individuality is an exciting new field, but no study to date has focused on characterizing the large-scale variance-covariance structure of IGV in behavior.
evidence: This is a knowledge gap statement based on the authors' assessment of the literature.

claim: Behavioral correlations within a genotype could arise through cell-to-cell variation in gene expression.
source: Behavioral correlations within a genotype could arise through a number of biological mechanisms including cell-to-cell variation in gene expression or individual differences in neural circuit wiring or synaptic weights.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential mechanisms.

claim: Behavioral correlations within a genotype could arise through individual differences in neural circuit wiring or synaptic weights.
source: Behavioral correlations within a genotype could arise through a number of biological mechanisms including cell-to-cell variation in gene expression or individual differences in neural circuit wiring or synaptic weights.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential mechanisms.

claim: Stochastic variation during developmental critical windows has the potential to impart lasting differences between individuals in the absence of conspicuous genetic or environmental differences.
source: For example, stochastic variation during developmental critical windows has the potential to impart lasting differences between individuals in the absence of conspicuous genetic or environmental differences.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential mechanisms based on developmental biology principles.

claim: The structure of intragenotypic behavioral variability will shape the distribution and kinds of personalities that a population of organisms displays.
source: The structure of intragenotypic behavioral variability (1) will shape the distribution and kinds of personalities that a population of organisms displays, even when they have matched genomes and environments
evidence: This is an inference about the implications of the research question.

claim: The structure of intragenotypic behavioral variability is the product of stochastic biological outcomes.
source: (2) is the product of stochastic biological outcomes, and its organization reveals how stochasticity drives variation
evidence: This is an inference about the nature of intragenotypic variation.

claim: The structure of intragenotypic behavioral variability constrains the evolution of behavior and adaptive phenotypic strategies like bet-hedging.
source: (3) constrains the evolution of behavior and adaptive phenotypic strategies like bet-hedging (Hopper, 1999)
evidence: This is an inference supported by a citation to Hopper, 1999.

claim: The structure of intragenotypic behavioral variability is a relatively uncharacterized component of neural diversity and its manifestations in behavior and disease.
source: (4) is a relatively uncharacterized component of neural diversity and its manifestations in behavior and disease
evidence: This is a knowledge gap statement.

claim: The structure of intragenotypic behavioral variability may shed light on how the nervous system orchestrates behavior as a whole.
source: (5) may shed light on how the nervous system orchestrates behavior as a whole.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential insights from the research.

claim: The experimental pipeline produced a data set of 200+ individual flies with many behavioral measurements each.
source: The first step in revealing the structure of behavioral variation within a genotype was to devise an experimental pipeline that produced a data set of many (200+) individual flies, with many behavioral measurements each.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: Six behavioral assays were implemented in a common experimental platform.
source: We developed a number of behavioral assays, measuring both spontaneous and stimulus-evoked responses of individual flies, which could be implemented in a common experimental platform (Figure 1A; Werkhoven et al., 2019). This instrument features an imaging plane, within which flies moved in arenas of various geometries. Fly position was tracked with digital cameras using diffused infrared illumination invisible to the flies. Visual stimuli were presented to the animals using DLP projectors or LEDs embedded in the arena walls. We implemented six assays (Supplementary file 1)
evidence: This describes the experimental methods and is supported by Figure 1A and a citation to Werkhoven et al., 2019.

claim: The behavioral assays assessed spontaneous walking in circular arenas.
source: We implemented six assays (Supplementary file 1) in this style, assessing (1) spontaneous walking in circular arenas
evidence: This describes one of the behavioral assays.

claim: The behavioral assays assessed preference to rest in brighter or dimmer positions in an environment of spatially structured illumination.
source: (2) preference to rest in brighter or dimmer positions (in an environment of spatially structured illumination)
evidence: This describes one of the behavioral assays.

claim: The behavioral assays assessed preference to rest in brighter or dimmer light levels in a fictive, temporally modulated light environment.
source: (3) preference to rest in brighter or dimmer light levels (in a fictive, temporally modulated light environment)
evidence: This describes one of the behavioral assays.

claim: The behavioral assays assessed optomotor responses to rotating visual stripes.
source: (4) optomotor responses to rotating visual stripes
evidence: This describes one of the behavioral assays.

claim: The behavioral assays assessed spontaneous left-right decision making in Y-mazes.
source: (5) spontaneous left-right decision making in Y-mazes
evidence: This describes one of the behavioral assays.

claim: The behavioral assays assessed phototaxis in Y-mazes where flies are given a choice of walking toward or away from a lit LED.
source: (6) phototaxis in Y-mazes, where flies are given a choice of walking toward or away from a lit LED (Figure 1B).
evidence: This describes one of the behavioral assays and references Figure 1B.

claim: The LED Y-maze assay yields multiple behavioral measures including the number of choices made, the fraction of turns that are to the right, the fraction of turns toward the lit LED, the number of pauses, and the average duration of pauses.
source: For example, flies behaving in the phototactic 'LED Y-maze' (assay 6) are performing phototaxis and exploratory locomotion but yield several different behavioral measures, including the number of choices made by passing through the choice point of the Y-maze (a measure of total activity), the fraction of turns that are to the right, the fraction of turns that are toward the lit LED, the number of pauses in which the animal did not move, the average duration of pauses, etc.
evidence: This describes the multiple measures obtained from a single assay.

claim: The total collection of behavioral measures across all assays per fly was up to 121.
source: Thus, the total collection of behavioral measures across all assays per fly was quite large (up to 121), constituting a diverse, inclusive characterization of individual behavior.
evidence: This describes the scope of data collection.

claim: The primary measures from each assay are consistent across days within an individual.
source: In control experiments, we confirmed that these primary measures are consistent across days within an individual (Figure 1—figure supplement 1; i.e., they reflect persistent idiosyncrasies [Kain et al., 2012; Buchanan et al., 2015; Kain et al., 2015; Honegger et al., 2020]).
evidence: This is a finding from control experiments, supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and citations.

claim: The Decathlon experimental pipeline lasted 13 consecutive days.
source: In order to obtain all of the behavioral measures from each experimental animal, we combined our behavioral assays in a serial experimental pipeline lasting 13 consecutive days (Figure 1C), generally with one unique assay per day and continuous circadian imaging (assay 9) between assays.
evidence: This describes the experimental timeline and is supported by Figure 1C.

claim: The Decathlon pipeline begins with 3-day-old flies being loaded into 96-well circadian imaging plates.
source: This pipeline begins with 3-day-old flies being loaded into the 96-well circadian imaging plates.
evidence: This describes the start of the experimental protocol.

claim: The most active 192 flies were retained for further testing after the first day of assays.
source: At this point, the most active 192 flies were retained for further testing. In preliminary experiments, we found that flies that were inactive at the beginning of the pipeline were very unlikely to produce substantial amounts of data over the rest of the pipeline.
evidence: This describes a selection step in the experimental protocol based on preliminary findings.

claim: The assay order was randomized between Decathlon implementations.
source: It is possible that the assay order has some effect on the recorded behavioral measures. So we randomized the assay order between Decathlon implementations as much as possible (Figure 1D), subject to two restrictions: activity screening was always the first assay, and high-resolution imaging for unsupervised analysis (assay 8) was always the last assay.
evidence: This describes the experimental design to control for order effects, supported by Figure 1D.

claim: When each fly completed all Decathlon assays, it was flash-frozen in liquid nitrogen for RNA sequencing.
source: When each fly completed its run through all Decathlon assays (i.e., over the 3 days of assay 8 imaging), it was flash-frozen in liquid nitrogen for RNA sequencing.
evidence: This describes the final step of the experimental protocol.

claim: Two Decathlons were conducted using highly inbred, nearly isogenic flies derived from the wild-type strain Berlin-K.
source: To collect data that would reveal the structure of behavioral variation within a genotype, we conducted two Decathlons using highly inbred, nearly isogenic flies derived from the wild-type strain Berlin-K (BSC#8522; Nöthel, 1981).
evidence: This describes the experimental subjects and is supported by a citation to Nöthel, 1981.

claim: The Berlin-K strain was confirmed to be highly isogenic with genomic sequencing showing ~75 SNPs across the entire genome.
source: We confirmed that this strain was, indeed, highly isogenic with genomic sequencing of individual animals, finding ~75 SNPs in the population across the entire genome (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from genomic sequencing, supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: 115 flies completed the first Decathlon.
source: 115 flies completed the first Decathlon, and 176 the second.
evidence: This reports the sample size for the first experiment.

claim: 176 flies completed the second Decathlon.
source: 115 flies completed the first Decathlon, and 176 the second.
evidence: This reports the sample size for the second experiment.

claim: Missing values in the data matrix were infilled using the alternating least-squares method.
source: We infilled missing values using the alternating least-squares method, which, as judged by analyses of toy ground truth data, performed better than mean-infilling (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This describes the data processing method and is supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: The correlation matrices of the two Berlin-Kiso Decathlon data sets were substantially more similar than expected by chance.
source: The correlation matrices of these two data sets were not identical, but were substantially more similar than expected by chance (Figure 1—figure supplement 6), implying that while there were inter-Decathlon effects, much of the same structure was present in each and merging them was justified.
evidence: This is a finding from statistical comparison, supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 6.

claim: The grand data matrix consisted of 382 individuals × 121 behavioral measures.
source: A grand data matrix was made by concatenating these batches (382 individuals × 121 behavioral measures).
evidence: This describes the final data matrix dimensions.

claim: The full correlation matrix of the Berlin-Kiso data set contains a substantial amount of structure.
source: The full correlation matrix of this Berlin-Kiso data set is shown in Figure 1E. It contains a substantial amount of structure, indicating that large groups of behavioral measures covary.
evidence: This is an observation from the correlation matrix shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Flies with higher variation in the inter-turn interval in the olfactory assay exhibited higher mean speed in the circadian assays.
source: For example, flies with higher variation in the inter-turn interval in the olfactory assay ('clumpiness' in their olfactory turning) exhibited higher mean speed in the circadian assays
evidence: This is a specific correlation observed in the data.

claim: Flies with higher variation in inter-turn intervals in the Y-maze exhibited lower mutual information in the direction of subsequent turns in the Y-maze.
source: and flies with higher variation in inter-turn intervals in the Y-maze (clumpiness in their Y-maze turning) exhibited lower mutual information in the direction of subsequent turns in the Y-maze ('switchiness' in their Y-maze handedness; Figure 1F. See below and Buchanan et al., 2015; Akhund-Zade et al., 2019) for more about these measures.
evidence: This is a specific correlation observed in the data, shown in Figure 1F and supported by citations.

claim: The distilled matrix reveals uncorrelated dimensions among measures for which there was a prior expectation of correlation.
source: To produce an exhaustive list of such non-trivial correlations, we distilled the grand correlation matrix to a smaller matrix (the 'distilled matrix'; Figure 1G) in which two kinds of interesting relationships were revealed: (1) uncorrelated dimensions among measures for which we had a prior expectation of correlation (e.g., if meanSpeed in circular arenas is found to be uncorrelated with meanSpeed in olfactory tunnels)
evidence: This describes the purpose and content of the distilled matrix shown in Figure 1G.

claim: The distilled matrix reveals correlated dimensions among measures for which there was no prior expectation of correlation.
source: and (2) correlated dimensions among measures for which we had no prior expectation of correlation.
evidence: This describes the purpose and content of the distilled matrix.

claim: The gravitaxis a priori group had 10 measures and only 2 significant PCs.
source: Some a priori groups largely matched our expectations, with relatively few uncorrelated dimensions among many measures (e.g., the gravitaxis group that had 10 measures and only 2 significant PCs)
evidence: This is a finding from the PCA analysis of a priori groups.

claim: The clumpiness a priori group had five measures and five significant PCs.
source: while others exhibited relatively many uncorrelated dimensions (e.g., the clumpiness group that had five measures and five significant PCs; see Figure 1—figure supplement 7 for all a priori group PCAs).
evidence: This is a finding from the PCA analysis of a priori groups, supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 7.

claim: The grand data matrix after distillation contained 38 behavioral measures.
source: With a priori group submatrices represented in their respective significant PCs, the grand data matrix now contained 38 behavioral measures.
evidence: This describes the dimensionality of the distilled data matrix.

claim: The distilled correlation matrix is sparse with most behavioral measures uncorrelated or weakly correlated.
source: The first impression of the distilled correlation matrix is that it is sparse. Most behavioral measures are uncorrelated or weakly correlated, suggesting that there are many independent dimensions of behavioral variation.
evidence: This is an observation from the distilled correlation matrix.

claim: 176 pairs of behaviors were significantly correlated at a false discovery rate of 38% in the distilled matrix.
source: However, 176 pairs of behaviors were significantly correlated at a false discovery rate (FDR) of 38%, and the distribution of p-values for the entries in this matrix exhibits a clear enrichment of low values (Figure 1—figure supplement 8), indicating an enrichment of significant correlations.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the distilled correlation matrix, supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 8.

claim: Flies with high values in the first PC of the phototaxis a priori group tend to have high values in the second PC of the activity level a priori group.
source: As an example, flies with high values in the first PC of the phototaxis a priori group tend to have high values in the second PC of the activity level a priori group.
evidence: This is a specific correlation observed in the distilled matrix.

claim: The third switchiness PC is positively correlated with the second clumpiness PC.
source: As another example, the third switchiness PC is positively correlated with the second clumpiness PC (Figure 1H; a relationship that is likely related to the positive correlation between the Y-maze hand clumpiness and Y-maze hand switchiness, Figure 1F).
evidence: This is a specific correlation observed in the distilled matrix, shown in Figure 1H.

claim: The correlation between the third switchiness PC and second clumpiness PC represents a correlation between olfactory tunnel turn direction switchiness and olfactory tunnel turn timing clumpiness.
source: Interpreting the loadings (Figure 1—figure supplements 9 and 10) of these PCs indicates that this is a correlation between olfactory tunnel turn direction switchiness and olfactory tunnel turn timing clumpiness.
evidence: This is an interpretation of PC loadings shown in Figure 1—figure supplements 9 and 10.

claim: A substantial number of correlations were detected between different dimensions of switchiness and clumpiness.
source: We detected a substantial number of correlations between different dimensions of switchiness and clumpiness (Figure 1—figure supplement 11), suggesting that there are multiple couplings between these suites of traits.
evidence: This is a finding from the correlation analysis, supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 11.

claim: The full matrix contained 22 significant PCs.
source: The full matrix contained 22 significant PCs, with PCs 1–3 explaining 9.3, 6.9, and 5.8% of the variance, respectively
evidence: This is a finding from PCA on the full matrix.

claim: PCs 1–3 of the full matrix explained 9.3, 6.9, and 5.8% of the variance, respectively.
source: The full matrix contained 22 significant PCs, with PCs 1–3 explaining 9.3, 6.9, and 5.8% of the variance, respectively
evidence: This is a finding from PCA on the full matrix.

claim: The distilled matrix contained 16 significant PCs.
source: (the distilled matrix contained 16 significant PCs, with PCs 1–3 explaining 13.8, 10.0, and 7.7% of the variance, respectively; Figure 1I).
evidence: This is a finding from PCA on the distilled matrix, shown in Figure 1I.

claim: PCs 1–3 of the distilled matrix explained 13.8, 10.0, and 7.7% of the variance, respectively.
source: (the distilled matrix contained 16 significant PCs, with PCs 1–3 explaining 13.8, 10.0, and 7.7% of the variance, respectively; Figure 1I).
evidence: This is a finding from PCA on the distilled matrix, shown in Figure 1I.

claim: The connected components spectrum of the distilled Decathlon data set had peaks at 1 and d.
source: The connected components spectrum (Figure 1J) of the distilled Decathlon data set had peaks at 1 and d (Li and Durbin, 2009).
evidence: This is a finding from the connected components analysis, shown in Figure 1J and supported by a citation.

claim: There was evidence for structure over the full range of intermediate dimensionalities in the connected components spectrum.
source: There was also evidence for structure over the full range of intermediate dimensionalities.
evidence: This is an observation from the connected components spectrum.

claim: The organization of behavioral variation is one of predominantly uncorrelated behaviors, with sparse sets of behaviors correlated with continuously varying strengths.
source: Overall, the organization is one of predominantly uncorrelated behaviors, with sparse sets of behaviors correlated with continuously varying strengths.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the connected components spectrum.

claim: Individual flies embedded in two dimensions using t-SNE appear continuously distributed around a single mode with no discrete clusters.
source: To assess how individual flies are distributed in behavior space, we embedded them from the 384-dimensional space into two dimensions using t-SNE (van der Maaten and Hinton, 2008). There appear to be no discrete clusters corresponding to 'types' of flies. Instead, variation among flies appears continuously distributed around a single mode (Figure 1K).
evidence: This is a finding from t-SNE embedding shown in Figure 1K, with the method supported by a citation.

claim: Behavioral measures embedded in two dimensions using t-SNE show that measures thought to be similar were often dissimilar across flies, and sometimes measures not anticipated to be similar were similar.
source: We also embedded behavioral measures as points from the 121-dimensional space of flies into two dimensions (Figure 1L). This confirmed that while our intuition for which sets of measures would be similar (the a priori groups) was right in many cases, measures we thought would be similar were often dissimilar across flies, and sometimes measures we did not anticipate being similar were (e.g., phototaxis and activity level).
evidence: This is a finding from t-SNE embedding shown in Figure 1L.

claim: High-speed, high-resolution video was acquired for flies at 100 Hz over 60 minutes.
source: Over 3 days, we acquired 13.5 GB of 200 × 200 px 100 Hz videos centered on each fly as they behaved spontaneously over the course of 60 min.
evidence: This describes the video acquisition parameters.

claim: An unsupervised analysis pipeline computed high-dimensional representations of video data in the time-frequency domain before embedding them in two dimensions and demarcating boundaries between 70 discrete modes of behavior.
source: These frames were fed into an unsupervised analysis pipeline (Berman et al., 2014) that computed high-dimensional representations of these data in the time-frequency domain before embedding them in two dimensions and demarcating boundaries between 70 discrete modes of behavior (Figure 2B).
evidence: This describes the unsupervised analysis method, shown in Figure 2B and supported by a citation to Berman et al., 2014.

claim: Flies exhibited a broadly similar probability distribution of performing each of the 70 unsupervised behavioral modes.
source: Flies exhibited a broadly similar probability distribution of performing each of these behaviors (Figure 2C), though there were conspicuous differences among individual patterns of behavior (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a finding from the unsupervised analysis, shown in Figures 2C and 2D.

claim: The correlation matrix of behavioral modes identified in the unsupervised analysis was highly structured.
source: The correlation matrix of behavioral modes identified in the unsupervised analysis was highly structured (Figure 2E; like the correlation matrix of the rest of the Decathlon measures, Figure 1E)
evidence: This is an observation from the correlation matrix shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The unsupervised behavioral modes appeared to be strongly organized in 10 or fewer dimensions.
source: appearing to be strongly organized in 10 or fewer dimensions, with some evidence of organization in higher dimensions (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is a finding from the connected components analysis shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Correlations between behavioral modes identified by unsupervised clustering and measures from other Decathlon assays were generally weaker than correlations within these categories, but were nevertheless enriched for significant relationships.
source: Correlations between behavioral modes identified by unsupervised clustering and measures from the other Decathlon assays were generally weaker than correlations within these categories, but were nevertheless enriched for significant relationships (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from correlation analysis, supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Highly correlated behavioral modes tended to reflect variations on the same type of behavior or behaviors performed on the same region of the body.
source: But, in examining sample movies of flies executing each of the 70 unsupervised behavioral modes (Videos 1–4), it was clear that highly correlated behavioral modes tended to reflect variations on the same type of behavior (e.g., walking) or behaviors performed on the same region of the body (e.g., anterior movements including eye and foreleg grooming; Figure 2G).
evidence: This is an observation from examining videos and the correlation structure, shown in Figure 2G and Videos 1–4.

claim: Individual flies that perform more eye grooming tend to perform more of other anterior behaviors.
source: In other words, individual flies that perform more eye grooming tend to perform more of other anterior behaviors.
evidence: This is an inference from the correlation patterns observed.

claim: Flies that spent more time performing anterior grooming also spent more time performing slow leg movements.
source: There were some correlations between behaviors implemented by disparate parts of the body. For example, flies that spent more time performing anterior grooming also spent more time performing slow leg movements (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is a specific correlation observed in the data, shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Behaviors whose prevalence covaries across individuals have similar time-frequency patterns across the body.
source: That is, behaviors whose prevalence covaries across individuals have similar time-frequency patterns across the body.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that covarying behaviors are contiguously embedded.

claim: Clusters of covarying, contiguously embedded behaviors exhibited similar temporal transitions.
source: Moreover, these clusters of covarying, contiguously embedded behaviors exhibited similar temporal transitions; behaviors that covary across individuals tend to precede specific sets of subsequent behaviors (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is a finding from the transition matrix analysis shown in Figure 2H.

claim: There appear to be couplings between the dimensions of behavioral variation across individuals, the domains of the body implementing behavior, and the temporal patterning of behaviors.
source: Thus, there appear to be couplings between the dimensions of behavioral variation across individuals, the domains of the body implementing behavior, and the temporal patterning of behaviors.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from multiple observations about behavioral correlations, body regions, and temporal transitions.

claim: A thermogenetic neural circuit perturbation screen was used to test correlations in the Decathlon matrices as hypotheses.
source: To (1) confirm that the Decathlon experiments revealed biologically meaningful couplings between behaviors and (2) probe biological mechanisms potentially giving rise to behavioral correlations, we treated correlations in the Decathlon matrices as hypotheses to test using data from a thermogenetic neural circuit perturbation screen (Skutt-Kakaria et al., 2019).
evidence: This describes the experimental approach and is supported by a citation to Skutt-Kakaria et al., 2019.

claim: The focus was on correlations between measures of turn timing clumpiness and turn direction switchiness.
source: Specifically, we focused on the many correlations between measures of turn timing clumpiness and turn direction switchiness (Figure 1H and S8).
evidence: This describes the specific correlations tested, referencing Figure 1H and S8.

claim: Before the Decathlon experiment, there was no reason to think clumpiness and switchiness measures would be correlated.
source: Before the Decathlon experiment, we had no reason to think these measures would be correlated, as one describes higher-order structure in the timing of locomotor turns (clumpiness), and the other describes higher-order structure in the direction of sequential turns (switchiness).
evidence: This is a statement about the authors' prior expectations.

claim: The prediction from the Decathlon was that if perturbing a circuit element caused a change in clumpiness it would tend to also cause a change in switchiness in a consistent direction.
source: Our prediction derived from the Decathlon was that if perturbing a circuit element caused a change in clumpiness it would tend to also cause a change in switchiness in a consistent direction.
evidence: This is a hypothesis derived from the Decathlon findings.

claim: Neurons in the central complex were inactivated or activated using Gal4 lines targeting single cell types.
source: We looked for such correlated changes when we inactivated or activated neurons in the central complex (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–C), a cluster of neuropils involved in locomotor behaviors (Buchanan et al., 2015; Ofstad et al., 2011; Kottler et al., 2019) and heading estimation (Seelig and Jayaraman, 2015; Green et al., 2017; Kakaria and de Bivort, 2017). We used a set of Gal4 lines (Wolff and Rubin, 2018), each of which targets a single cell type and that tile the entire protocerebral bridge (a central complex neuropil; see Supplementary file 4), to express Shibirets (Kitamoto, 2001) or dTRPA1 (Hamada et al., 2008), thermogenetic reagents that block vesicular release and depolarize cells, respectively.
evidence: This describes the experimental manipulation, supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–C and multiple citations.

claim: At the permissive temperature, significant negative correlations were observed in the average line clumpiness and switchiness of control and dTrpA1 expressing lines.
source: At the permissive temperature, we observed significant negative correlations in the average line clumpiness and switchiness of control and dTrpA1 expressing lines (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D and E).
evidence: This is a finding from the thermogenetic screen, shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D and E.

claim: The mechanisms that couple variation in switchiness and clumpiness within a genotype may also be at play across genotypes.
source: This suggests that the mechanisms that couple variation in switchiness and clumpiness within a genotype may also be at play across genotypes.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation of negative correlations at permissive temperature.

claim: At the restrictive temperature, significant positive correlations between clumpiness and switchiness were observed in all three experimental treatments: control, Gal4/Shibirets, and Gal4/dTRPA1 lines.
source: Surprisingly, at the restrictive temperature, we saw significant positive correlations between clumpiness and switchiness in all three experimental treatments: control (Gal4/+), Gal4/Shibirets, and Gal4/dTRPA1 lines.
evidence: This is a finding from the thermogenetic screen.

claim: Temperature alone can selectively alter the function of circuit elements regulating both clumpiness and switchiness, effectively reversing their coupling.
source: That this correlation appeared in controls suggests that temperature alone can selectively alter the function of circuit elements regulating both clumpiness and switchiness, effectively reversing their coupling.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that the correlation reversal occurred in controls.

claim: Perturbing neurons in the central complex can block temperature-induced changes in the coupling of clumpiness and switchiness.
source: The dTrpA1- and Shibirets-expressing lines also showed this reversal, but to a lesser extent, suggesting that perturbing neurons in the central complex can block temperature-induced changes in the coupling of clumpiness and switchiness.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that the reversal was less pronounced in experimental lines.

claim: RNA sequencing was performed on the heads of flies at the end of the first Decathlon experiment.
source: To test this hypothesis, we performed RNA sequencing on the heads of the flies at the end of the first Decathlon experiment (Figure 3A).
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure, shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Tm3′seq was used to make 3′-biased libraries for each individual animal.
source: We used Tm3′seq (Pallares et al., 2020) to make 3′-biased libraries for each individual animal.
evidence: This describes the sequencing method and is supported by a citation to Pallares et al., 2020.

claim: The expression of 17,470 genes was quantified in 101 individual flies.
source: We quantified the expression of 17,470 genes in 101 individual flies.
evidence: This reports the scope of the transcriptomic data.

claim: The expression profiles were strongly correlated across individuals.
source: The expression profiles were strongly correlated across individuals (Figure 3B), but there was some significant variation across individuals (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a finding from the transcriptomic analysis, shown in Figures 3B and 3C.

claim: Linear models were trained to predict an individual's behavioral measures from its transcriptional idiosyncrasies.
source: To assess whether this variation was meaningful with respect to behavioral variation, we trained linear models (over 625,000 in total) to predict an individual's behavioral measures from its transcriptional idiosyncrasies. Specifically, we fit simple linear models for each of our 97 behavioral measures as a function of the 6642 most highly expressed genes.
evidence: This describes the modeling approach.

claim: The median model had an r2 value of 0.008%.
source: The median model had an r2 value of 0.008% and 5% of models predicted behavior at r2 > 0.135.
evidence: This is a finding from the linear modeling.

claim: 5% of models predicted behavior at r2 > 0.135.
source: The median model had an r2 value of 0.008% and 5% of models predicted behavior at r2 > 0.135.
evidence: This is a finding from the linear modeling.

claim: Behavioral measures varied greatly in their number of significant gene predictors, ranging from 147 to 1172 genes.
source: Behavioral measures varied greatly in their number of significant (p<0.05) gene predictors (Figure 3D), ranging from 147 to 1172 genes.
evidence: This is a finding from the linear modeling, shown in Figure 3D.

claim: 37 KEGG pathways were significantly enriched in the genes that predicted individual behavioral measures.
source: Across all behaviors, we found that 37 KEGG pathways were significantly enriched in the genes that predicted individual behavioral measures (Figure 3E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is a finding from the KEGG enrichment analysis, shown in Figure 3E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Many of the enriched KEGG pathways were significantly enriched compared to shuffled controls and were enriched in multiple behavioral measures.
source: Many of these pathways were significantly enriched compared to shuffled controls and were enriched in multiple behavioral measures (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is a finding from the KEGG enrichment analysis, shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The significance of pathway enrichments was highly correlated (r = 0.87) between the first and second Decathlon experiments.
source: We repeated this experiment and analysis on flies of the second Decathlon experiment and found that the significance of pathway enrichments was highly correlated (r = 0.87; Figure 3G)
evidence: This is a finding from comparing enrichment analyses across experiments, shown in Figure 3G.

claim: 43% of significant KEGG pathways in the first Decathlon experiment were shared in the second experiment.
source: with 43 and 73% of significant KEGG pathways in the first and second Decathlon experiments (respectively) shared in the other experiment.
evidence: This is a finding from comparing enrichment analyses across experiments.

claim: 73% of significant KEGG pathways in the second Decathlon experiment were shared in the first experiment.
source: with 43 and 73% of significant KEGG pathways in the first and second Decathlon experiments (respectively) shared in the other experiment.
evidence: This is a finding from comparing enrichment analyses across experiments.

claim: Genes related to cellular respiration were significantly enriched for multiple behavioral measures.
source: Genes related to cellular respiration, protein translation, and phototransduction were significantly enriched for multiple behavioral measures, a result that was highly robust to bootstrap resampling.
evidence: This is a finding from the KEGG enrichment analysis.

claim: Genes related to protein translation were significantly enriched for multiple behavioral measures.
source: Genes related to cellular respiration, protein translation, and phototransduction were significantly enriched for multiple behavioral measures, a result that was highly robust to bootstrap resampling.
evidence: This is a finding from the KEGG enrichment analysis.

claim: Genes related to phototransduction were significantly enriched for multiple behavioral measures.
source: Genes related to cellular respiration, protein translation, and phototransduction were significantly enriched for multiple behavioral measures, a result that was highly robust to bootstrap resampling.
evidence: This is a finding from the KEGG enrichment analysis.

claim: Cellular respiration was the most common enrichment, significant in 11 of 97 behavioral measures.
source: Cellular respiration was the most common enrichment, significant in 11 of 97 behavioral measures, suggesting that variation in metabolic rate may be predictive of variation in many behaviors.
evidence: This is a finding from the KEGG enrichment analysis.

claim: Variation in metabolic rate may be predictive of variation in many behaviors.
source: Cellular respiration was the most common enrichment, significant in 11 of 97 behavioral measures, suggesting that variation in metabolic rate may be predictive of variation in many behaviors.
evidence: This is an inference from the enrichment of cellular respiration genes.

claim: 24 of 37 significant KEGG categories were related to metabolism.
source: Indeed, metabolic function was a common link between significant categories, with a total of 24 of 37 being related to metabolism.
evidence: This is a finding from the KEGG enrichment analysis.

claim: 11 enriched pathways were associated with protein turnover.
source: We also found 11 pathways (including two highly enriched categories: ribosome and proteasome) associated with protein turnover.
evidence: This is a finding from the KEGG enrichment analysis.

claim: Enriched pathways including Hedgehog signaling, Wnt signaling, insect hormone biosynthesis, SNARE vesicular transport, and phototransduction suggested roles for development and neuronal function in individual behavioral variation.
source: While most enriched pathways were related to basic cellular processes, others (Hedgehog signaling, Wnt signaling, insect hormone biosynthesis, SNARE vesicular transport, and phototransduction) suggested roles for development and neuronal function in individual behavioral variation.
evidence: This is an inference from the KEGG enrichment analysis.

claim: A Decathlon experiment was conducted on outbred flies from a synthetic genetic mapping population.
source: We tested this by conducting a Decathlon experiment on outbred flies (n = 192) from a synthetic genetic mapping population (Long et al., 2014).
evidence: This describes the experimental design and is supported by a citation to Long et al., 2014.

claim: The outbred flies were from a high (~100)-generation intercross population seeded by eight kinds of F1 heterozygotes produced by round-robin cross from eight inbred wild strains.
source: These animals were from a high (~100)-generation intercross population ('NEX'; seeded in the first generation by eight kinds of F1 heterozygotes produced by round-robin cross from eight inbred wild strains).
evidence: This describes the genetic background of the outbred flies.

claim: The distilled correlation matrix of outbred flies appears qualitatively similar to that of inbred animals.
source: A distilled correlation matrix of behavioral measures (Figure 4A) was produced by the same method as above. At first glance, it appears qualitatively similar to the distilled correlation matrix from inbred animals (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is an observation from comparing correlation matrices shown in Figures 4A and 1G.

claim: In inbred and outbred populations, individuals do not fall into discrete clusters as determined by t-SNE embedding.
source: In inbred and outbred populations, (1) individuals do not fall into discrete clusters, as determined by t-SNE embedding of individuals as points (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a finding from t-SNE embedding shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Inbred and outbred flies appear to lie on the same manifold in behavioral measure space.
source: Moreover inbred and outbred flies appear to lie on the same manifold in behavioral measure space
evidence: This is an observation from the t-SNE embedding.

claim: Behavioral measures cluster according to their membership in a priori groups similarly in outbred and inbred populations.
source: (2) behavioral measures cluster according to their membership in a priori groups similarly in outbred (Figure 4C) and inbred (Figure 1L) populations
evidence: This is a finding from t-SNE embedding of measures shown in Figures 4C and 1L.

claim: The distribution of percent variance explained by PC was similar in inbred and outbred populations.
source: (3) the distribution of percent variance explained by PC was similar (Figure 4D)
evidence: This is a finding from PCA shown in Figure 4D.

claim: There is a similar connected components spectrum in inbred and outbred populations, with substantial distribution of behavioral biases across the full d dimensions and a sparse network of correlations.
source: (4) there is a similar connected components spectrum, with substantial distribution of behavioral biases across the full d dimensions and a sparse network of correlations coupling behaviors over a continuum of dimensionalities (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is a finding from the connected components analysis shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Correlated clusters of unsupervised behavior modes from outbred flies corresponded broadly to the clusters mapped to anatomical regions in inbred flies.
source: Correlated clusters of unsupervised behavior modes from outbred flies corresponded broadly to the clusters mapped to anatomical regions in inbred flies (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the unsupervised analysis, shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The behaviors of outbred flies were broadly correlated to gene expression, similar to inbred flies.
source: We further conducted transcriptomic sequencing and analysis on the heads of these outbred flies and found that, similar to the inbred flies, their behaviors were broadly correlated to gene expression (Figure 4—figure supplement 2, Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a finding from the transcriptomic analysis, shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2 and Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: The percent of significant pathways overlapping between pairs of inbred and outbred Decathlon experiments was similar to that of pairs of inbred Decathlon experiments, ranging from 38% to 64%.
source: The percent of significant pathways overlapping between pairs of inbred and outbred Decathlon experiments was similar to that of pairs of inbred Decathlon experiments, ranging from 38% to 64%.
evidence: This is a finding from comparing KEGG enrichment analyses across experiments.

claim: The correlation coefficient between the inbred and outbred populations in the pairwise correlations between behavioral measures is statistically significant (p=0.001) but low in magnitude (r = 0.11).
source: There appears to be some similarity at this level (Figure 4F); the correlation coefficient between the inbred and outbred populations in the pairwise correlations between behavioral measures is statistically significant (p=0.001), but low in magnitude (r = 0.11).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from comparing correlation matrices, shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The correlations between specific behaviors are sometimes the same between inbred and outbred animals, but sometimes not.
source: Examining specific pairs of scatter plots, it is clear that the correlations between specific behaviors are sometimes the same between the inbred and outbred animals, but sometimes not (Figure 4G, Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is an observation from comparing specific correlations, shown in Figure 4G and Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: Four data sets were examined to compare the correlation structure of behavior from different sources of variation: BABAM, DGRP behavioral, DGRP physiological, and split-Gal4 DN.
source: Lastly, we examined how the correlation structure of behavior compared between sets of flies with variation coming from different sources. Specifically, we looked at four data sets: (1) the BABAM data set (Robie et al., 2017), in which measures were acquired from groups of flies behaving in open arenas, and variation came from the thermogenetic activation of 2381 different sets of neurons (the first-generation FlyLight Gal4 lines Jenett et al., 2012); (2) a Drosophila Genome Reference Panel (DGRP; Mackay et al., 2012) behavioral data set, in which measures were acquired in behavioral assays similar to the Decathlon experiments (sometimes manually, sometimes automatically), and variation came from the natural genetic variation between lines in the DGRP collection; (3) a DGRP physiological data set, in which measures are physiological or metabolic (e.g., body weight and glucose levels) and variation came from the natural genetic variation between lines in the DGRP collection; and (4) the split-Gal4 Descending Neuron (DN) data set (Cande et al., 2018) in which measures came from the same unsupervised cluster approach as Figure 2, and variation came from the optogenetic activation of specific sets of descending neurons projecting from the brain to the ventral nerve cord (Namiki et al., 2018).
evidence: This describes the data sets analyzed and is supported by multiple citations.

claim: All of the external data sets show substantial structure in their correlation matrices.
source: All of these data sets show substantial structure in their correlation matrices (Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an observation from the correlation matrices shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The BABAM and DN correlation matrices contain numerous high correlation values, indicative of strong couplings between behaviors under neuronal manipulations.
source: The BABAM and especially the DN correlation matrices contain numerous high correlation values, indicative of strong couplings between behaviors under these neuronal manipulations.
evidence: This is an observation from the correlation matrices.

claim: The DGRP correlation matrices look more qualitatively similar to the Decathlon matrix, with lower, sparser correlations.
source: The DGRP correlation matrices, especially the DGRP behavioral matrix, look more qualitatively similar to the Decathlon matrix, with lower, sparser correlations.
evidence: This is an observation from comparing correlation matrices.

claim: Behavioral variation has coarsely similar structure whether variation arises intragenotypically, intergenotypically among outbred individuals, or intergenotypically among inbred lines derived from wild populations.
source: This suggests that behavioral variation has coarsely similar structure whether variation arises intragenotypically (e.g., through stochastic variation in transcription; Figures 3B and 1J), intergenotypically among outbred individuals (Figure 4E), or intergenotypically among inbred lines derived from wild populations (Figure 5A2).
evidence: This is an inference from comparing correlation structures across data sets, referencing multiple figures.

claim: The connected components spectra of the external data sets are similar in offering evidence of organization over a wide range of dimensionalities, including high dimensionalities.
source: The connected components spectra of these matrices (Figure 5B) are similar in offering evidence of organization over a wide range of dimensionalities, including high dimensionalities.
evidence: This is a finding from the connected components analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Only the BABAM spectrum has no power at the dimensionality of its raw count of measurements.
source: Only the BABAM spectrum has no power at the dimensionality of its raw count of measurements.
evidence: This is an observation from the connected components spectrum.

claim: The BABAM and DN spectra have a single predominant peak at dimensionality = 1.
source: The BABAM and DN spectra have a single predominant peak (at dimensionality = 1), suggesting that most measures belong to a single network of at least weak couplings.
evidence: This is a finding from the connected components analysis.

claim: The DGRP physiology data exhibits weak peaks at dimensionality = 1 and d, but also peaks at ~25 and 37 dimensions.
source: The DGRP physiology data exhibits weak peaks at dimensionality = 1 and d, but also peaks at ~25 and 37 dimensions, suggesting that intergenotypic variation in physiology may have an intrinsic dimensionality in that range.
evidence: This is a finding from the connected components analysis.

claim: The spectrum of the DGRP behavior data looks similar to that of the Decathlons, with peaks at dimensionality = 1 and d, and evidence for structure over the full range of intermediate dimensionalities.
source: The spectrum of the DGRP behavior data looks similar to that of the Decathlons, with peaks at dimensionality = 1 and d, and evidence for structure over the full range of intermediate dimensionalities.
evidence: This is a finding from the connected components analysis.

claim: No evidence for low-dimensional organization was found in either DGRP data set.
source: Ultimately, we found no evidence for low-dimensional organization in either DGRP data set.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the connected components analysis.

claim: The distribution of individual lines in the space of DGRP behavior and physiology measures appears to be distributed single mode.
source: The distribution of individual lines in the space of DGRP behavior (and physiology) measures appears to be distributed single mode (Figure 5C2 and C3), like individual flies in the Decathlon (Figure 1K).
evidence: This is a finding from t-SNE embedding shown in Figure 5C2 and C3.

claim: There is some organization of individual lines in the BABAM and DN data sets, likely reflecting neuronal perturbations affecting multiple circuit elements mediating the same behavior(s).
source: In contrast, there is some organization of individual lines in the BABAM and DN data sets, likely reflecting neuronal perturbations affecting multiple circuit elements mediating the same behavior(s) (e.g., multiple lines targeting the same neuropil).
evidence: This is an observation from t-SNE embedding with an inference about the cause.

claim: Measures fall into clusters in all external data sets except the DGRP behavioral measures.
source: Measures fall into clusters in all of these data sets except the DGRP behavioral measures (Figure 5D), which appear distributed around a single mode, perhaps reflecting the high dimensionality of behavior itself.
evidence: This is a finding from t-SNE embedding shown in Figure 5D.

claim: This work represents the most complete characterization to date of the structure of behavioral variation within a genotype.
source: This work represents the most complete characterization to date of the structure of behavioral variation within a genotype.
evidence: This is a summary claim about the significance of the work.

claim: There are no discrete types of flies.
source: We found that there are no discrete types of flies, and there are many independent dimensions of behavioral variation.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from t-SNE embeddings.

claim: There are many independent dimensions of behavioral variation.
source: We found that there are no discrete types of flies, and there are many independent dimensions of behavioral variation.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from PCA and connected components analyses.

claim: The similar organization of biological variation within and among genotypes suggests that fluctuations in the same biological processes underpin behavioral variation at both of these levels.
source: Moreover, the similar organization of biological variation within and among genotypes suggests that fluctuations in the same biological processes underpin behavioral variation at both of these levels.
evidence: This is an inference from the similarity of correlation structures across inbred and outbred populations.
